title: Summarize by group

outcomes.can: Produce one summary row per group.
Filter rows before grouping and groups after it.
Read the error from an aggregate in WHERE.
Group, filter the groups and sort by the summary.

intro: One total for the whole table is rarely enough. Reports want a total for each country, each department, each status. GROUP BY produces one summary row per group, and HAVING chooses which groups to keep.

steps.title: One row per group
steps.text: GROUP BY country sorts the rows into groups that share a country, then returns one row for each group. The SELECT list of a grouped query can hold two kinds of thing: the columns you grouped by, and aggregates. Each aggregate is worked out separately for every group. A plain column that is not in the GROUP BY is an error, for the same reason as in the last module: a group has many values of it.

steps.title: Count the groups
steps.text: Twenty customers live in nine countries. Predict how many rows come back.

steps.title: Follow the groups
steps.text: There is one row per country, so nine rows. count(*) is counted inside each group: 7 customers in the USA, 3 in Canada, and so on. ORDER BY runs last and can sort by an aggregate or by its alias. Here it puts the largest group first and breaks ties by country name.

steps.title: WHERE before, HAVING after
steps.text: A grouped query can filter at two points. WHERE filters rows before they are grouped, so it cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters the groups after the aggregates are worked out, so it can. The clauses are written in this order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY.

steps.title: Keep the large groups
steps.text: Departments have 1, 11, 4, 3 and 4 employees, and one employee has no department. Predict which department_id values appear.

steps.title: Follow the HAVING
steps.text: The rows are grouped by department_id, and count(*) and the average salary are worked out for each group. HAVING then keeps the groups with at least four rows: departments 2, 3 and 5. The group of one employee with a NULL department_id exists too, and is dropped with the other small groups.

steps.title: An aggregate in WHERE
steps.text: This query tries to keep the large groups with WHERE. Read it before checking.

steps.title: Read the error
steps.text: Check the example. Error 42803 says aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE. WHERE runs before the groups exist, so there is nothing to count yet. Move the test to HAVING, after GROUP BY.

steps.title: Count customers per country
steps.text: The starter groups by too much, so it returns one row per city.

steps.title: Find the well-stocked categories
steps.text: Work from the prompt. One test belongs in WHERE and one in HAVING.

choices.feedback: GROUP BY returns one row per group, not one per customer.
There is one row for each country.
Without GROUP BY the count would be one row. With it, each country gets its own.
Those departments have 11, 4 and 4 employees. HAVING keeps groups of four or more.
The test is count(*) >= 4, and two departments have exactly 4.
HAVING removes the groups with fewer than four employees.

questions.prompt: What happens when you check this example?

choices.text: It returns the countries with more than two customers.
choices.feedback: WHERE cannot use count(*). The statement fails.
The statement does not run. An aggregate in WHERE is an error.

choices.text: PostgreSQL reports an error on line 3.
choices.feedback: WHERE runs before grouping, so it cannot use an aggregate (42803). The test belongs in HAVING.

review.evidence: Open a fresh starter on a later visit, with the earlier answer closed. A first unaided pass on every case is later evidence of the skill. A hinted pass stays recorded as assisted.

drillGap: These drills practise one grouping feature each. They do not place one test in WHERE and another in HAVING.
